name: Raw eggs / oysters / zinc-rich foods
lead: Raw eggs, oysters and other zinc-rich foods are eaten by some people as part of a diet aimed at supporting testosterone and, through it, a leaner, more muscular and more masculine physique. The reasoning rests mainly on zinc, a mineral the body needs to produce testosterone, and on the long bodybuilding tradition of eating large quantities of eggs and shellfish for muscle gain [1][2][14][16].

Reference texts report that zinc deficiency can lower circulating testosterone, and that supplementing zinc beyond adequate intake does not change serum levels [1][2]. Oysters are described as by far the richest dietary source of zinc, and two oysters are said to cover a day's recommended zinc and vitamin B12 [2][18]. Eggs, raw or cooked, are valued by lifters mainly as an inexpensive protein and choline source rather than as a zinc source.

On looksmax.org, raw eggs are a recurring topic: members post about drinking a dozen or more at a time, ask about taste and safety, and argue over whether raw eggs offer anything cooked eggs do not [9][10][11][13]. Food-safety reviews and public-health agencies describe infection risks linked to raw shellfish and raw eggs, which is part of how experts discuss the practice [4][5][3][20].

paras: The practice sits at the meeting point of three ideas common in physique and masculinity-focused communities: that testosterone drives muscle, leanness and facial and body masculinity; that diet can support or limit it; and that traditional strength foods such as eggs, shellfish and organ meats carry the nutrients that matter. Followers eat oysters or other zinc-rich foods to keep zinc intake from being the limiting factor in testosterone production, and eat large numbers of eggs, often raw and blended, as a cheap source of protein, fat and choline [1][2][10][11].

The chain proponents describe runs from food to nutrient adequacy, to normal hormone production, to better training adaptation and a leaner, more muscular build. Reference texts describe the first links where zinc was lacking to begin with, and say little about eggs and oysters beyond their nutrient content [1][2][3].

Zinc is required to produce testosterone, and deficiency can reduce levels, potentially leading to hypogonadism and delayed puberty [2]. A 1963 case report described a young man whose stunted growth and underdeveloped genitalia reversed with zinc supplementation [2]. The testosterone article similarly says zinc deficiency lowers testosterone, while over-supplementation does not change serum levels [1].

Wikipedia's zinc article describes zinc as the second most abundant trace metal in the human body after iron, notes that inadequate intake affects an estimated two billion people in the developing world, and lists stunted growth and delayed sexual maturation among the effects of deficiency in children [19]. The same article says that taking in too much zinc can cause ataxia, lethargy and copper deficiency [19]. This distinction between correcting a shortfall and adding to an adequate intake is the point where proponents and reference texts most often diverge.

A 3-ounce serving of fried oysters is reported to contain about 74 mg of zinc, compared with about 7 mg in the same amount of braised beef chuck; other sources include crab, beef, cashews, lobster, pork and almonds [2]. Phytates in whole grains can reduce zinc absorption [2]. Wikipedia's oyster article describes oysters as rich in zinc, iron, calcium, selenium and vitamins A and B12, with roughly 9 g of protein per 100 g for Pacific oysters [18].
Eggs are a source of protein and choline. Wikipedia's egg article lists about 294 mg of choline per 100 g of hard-boiled whole egg [3].

Eating raw eggs is associated in popular culture with strength athletes. Bodybuilder and trainer Vince Gironda (1917 to 1997), nicknamed the Iron Guru, opened Vince's Gym in North Hollywood in 1948 and came second at the 1951 Mr. America contest [16]. He promoted a low-carbohydrate, high-fat plan sometimes called the steak and eggs diet, built around eggs, butter, cream, milk and red meat, and claimed that very large amounts of fertile eggs could rival the anabolic steroid Dianabol, while opposing steroid use [16]. A T Nation poster recalls the same coach promoting a high-egg diet, with raw eggs, on the premise that eggs supply what the body needs for hormones and gains [14].

Oysters carry an older reputation. Wikipedia reports that they have long been regarded as aphrodisiacs and that researchers have pointed to amino acids in bivalves that may affect sex hormone levels, while their zinc content is linked to testosterone production [18]. Shell middens show people have eaten oysters for thousands of years, and in nineteenth-century New York they were cheap working-class food before overharvesting made them a delicacy [18].

Looksmax.org threads show members drinking or blending raw eggs in quantities of a dozen or more, sometimes with milk [12][13][11]. In one thread a member who had been eating six pasteurised eggs a day for three months asked whether to switch to raw and whether bacteria or parasites were a concern [9]. Another thread argues that raw eggs are not worth the trouble, listing less protein per egg, less bioavailability and more taste complaints, and says the only reason to choose raw is choline content [10]. Replies in that thread say that adding raw eggs to a shake is simply easier than cooking [10].

Wikipedia reports that raw egg protein is about 51 percent bioavailable versus about 91 percent for cooked egg [3]. Raw egg white also contains avidin, a protein that binds the B vitamin biotin very tightly; its structure holds up below about 70 degrees Celsius and breaks down quickly toward 85 degrees, and a 1991 assay found that fried, poached and briefly boiled whites kept only a fraction of raw-egg activity [17].

A 2022 randomised trial in the Journal of Nutrition, titled in reference to the film Rocky, assigned 45 healthy resistance-trained young men after a whole-body workout to a recovery meal of five raw eggs, five boiled eggs (each about 30 g protein) or a low-protein control breakfast, and measured muscle protein synthesis with tracer infusion and muscle biopsies [8]. Peak plasma essential amino acids were about 20 percent higher after boiled than raw eggs, but post-exercise myofibrillar protein synthesis rose by about 20 percent after raw eggs and 18 percent after boiled eggs versus control, with no significant difference between the two preparations [8].

Wikipedia cites a 2002 US Department of Agriculture estimate that about 2.3 million of 69 billion eggs produced annually, roughly one in 30,000, were contaminated with Salmonella, and says the shell acts as a barrier that cracks or unhealthy hens can compromise [15]. Health experts quoted there advise that people particularly susceptible to salmonellosis, such as the elderly, pregnant women and the infirm, avoid raw eggs [3][15].

Oysters are often eaten raw on the half shell, and because they filter water they can concentrate bacteria; Wikipedia notes that warm-month Vibrio vulnificus infections can be deadly for people with weakened immune systems, and that holding oysters in clean water for 48 to 72 hours (depuration) is a common safety practice [18]. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says most vibriosis follows eating raw or undercooked shellfish, especially oysters; it describes V. vulnificus infections as severe, with roughly one in five affected people dying, and lists liver disease, cancer, diabetes, HIV, immune-suppressing treatment and stomach-acid-reducing medicines among risk factors [20].

Reviews likewise note that Vibrio infections, which live in marine environments, most often follow shellfish consumption, especially oysters, and that such infections are increasing in the United States [4]. A 2022 review describes filter-feeding molluscs as able to accumulate pathogenic microorganisms, with outbreaks reported more often as consumption has risen [5]. Mollusc allergy, driven mainly by the muscle protein tropomyosin, is also documented [6].

No studies found testing raw eggs, oysters or zinc-rich foods as a testosterone or physique intervention in men with normal zinc status. Related research includes work on zinc deficiency and testosterone summarised in reference texts [1][2], a 2022 randomized trial on raw eggs and postexercise recovery in healthy young men [8], and a 1990 controlled feeding trial in 18 men in which oyster, clam, crab and mussel diets lowered some blood lipids when eaten with moderate fat restriction [7].

lore.intro: Raw eggs appear on looksmax.org as a cheap high-protein, high-choline habit, with threads from members drinking large numbers at once and others asking whether it is safe or worthwhile [9][10][11][13]. Oysters are discussed as a zinc source for testosterone.

claims.claim: Drinking raw eggs is a cheap way to eat a lot of protein and choline
claims.believers: Members describe blending or drinking a dozen or more raw eggs for convenience, and one poster says raw eggs are the best choline source [10][11][13].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports raw egg protein is about 51 percent bioavailable versus about 91 percent cooked, and that health authorities advise against raw eggs for susceptible groups because of Salmonella [3].

claims.claim: Eggs supply what the body needs for hormones and gains
claims.believers: A T Nation poster recalls Vince Gironda pitching a very high daily egg intake, raw, on the premise that eggs contain the nutrients to get hormones right for gaining [14].
claims.experts: Reference texts link testosterone to zinc status rather than egg intake, and say supplementation beyond adequacy does not raise serum testosterone [1][2].

claims.claim: Oysters and other zinc-rich foods raise testosterone
claims.believers: Proponents point to zinc's role in testosterone production and oysters' very high zinc content [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports deficiency lowers testosterone but zinc supplementation above adequacy has no effect on serum levels [1][2].

claims.claim: Raw eggs are no better than cooked
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster calls raw eggs less nutritious, less tasty and not worth skipping the cooking, citing studies supporting cooked eggs [10].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports higher protein bioavailability for cooked egg [3].

claims.claim: Raw eggs build muscle as well as cooked eggs
claims.believers: Lifters who add raw eggs to shakes argue they deliver the same protein with less effort, a tradition popularised by strength-sport lore [11][14].
claims.experts: The 2022 randomised trial found muscle protein synthesis after exercise did not differ significantly between raw and boiled eggs, though raw eggs blunted the plasma amino acid peak [8]; Wikipedia reports lower protein bioavailability for raw egg [15].

claims.claim: Raw egg white's avidin blocks biotin, so raw eggs backfire
claims.believers: Raw-egg eaters generally say the volumes they drink are fine and point to the strength-sport tradition of raw eggs [14].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports avidin binds biotin extremely tightly and that heating reduces its activity, with loss accelerating above about 70 degrees Celsius [17].

claims.claim: Very large daily egg intake can rival anabolic drugs
claims.believers: Vince Gironda is reported to have claimed that very large amounts of fertile eggs could rival Dianabol [16].
claims.experts: No controlled study has tested high-volume egg intake against anabolic steroids; the randomised raw-egg trial examined a single post-workout meal in healthy men [8].

claims.claim: Raw oysters are a safe way to load up on zinc
claims.believers: Members and lifters present oysters as the most zinc-dense food [2][18].
claims.experts: The CDC reports most vibriosis follows raw or undercooked shellfish, and that V. vulnificus infections are severe with roughly one in five affected people dying [20][4].

card.summary: Oysters and eggs for testosterone via zinc; deficiency lowers T, but extra zinc is reported not to raise it further.
card.note: Raw animal foods carry general food-safety considerations.

quick.overview:
Some people eat oysters, raw eggs and other zinc-rich foods hoping to raise testosterone.
Reference texts say zinc is needed to make testosterone and deficiency lowers it, but that extra zinc beyond adequacy does not change serum levels.
quick.mechanism: Zinc is required for testosterone production, so correcting a shortfall may restore levels [2]. Oysters are an unusually zinc-dense food [2].
quick.risks: No harms from zinc-rich foods are described. Raw eggs and raw shellfish are not addressed in them.
